unit.title: The biases that cost you money
unit.description: The mental shortcuts that make you buy high, sell low and think you're a genius

u27l1.title: Your brain isn't built for investing

steps.title: Two ways of thinking
steps.body:
Daniel Kahneman, Nobel Prize in Economics:

• **System 1:** fast, intuitive and emotional. Perfect for dodging a car.
• **System 2:** slow, analytical and effortful. Needed to work out an expected value.

In the stock market, big decisions tend to be made with system 1: in fear, in a hurry or in euphoria.

steps.title: The investor gap
steps.body:
Morningstar, 10 years to 2025:

• US funds returned **9.9 %** a year.
• Their investors' money, flowing in and out, returned **8.7 %**: **1.2 points less** a year.
• In the most volatile funds the gap was −2.1 points; in the calm ones, −0.4.
• In spot bitcoin ETFs: investors **−5.8 %** versus **+8.5 %** for the ETF.

steps.title: Your takeaway
steps.body: The product can be good. The problem is behaviour: buying after the rises and selling after the falls.
steps.key: The brain runs from danger and follows the crowd: in the market, that means selling in the falls and buying in the euphoria.
steps.tip: The biggest risk to your portfolio is usually the person sitting in front of the screen.

steps.title: Losing hurts twice as much
steps.body:
Kahneman and Tversky (prospect theory, 1979): a loss of €100 hurts roughly **twice as much** as a gain of €100 feels good.

That's why we turn down bets that are in our favour and avoid **locking in** a loss by selling, even when the company has got worse.

steps.title: Its effects
steps.body:
• When we're losing, we become **more reckless**: «I'll double up to win it back».
• When we're winning, **more cautious**: we sell quickly to lock it in.
• If we check our portfolio very often, we see it in the red more times and suffer more: Benartzi and Thaler called this **myopic loss aversion**.

steps.title: How to protect yourself
steps.body: Set your stop before you get in, while you're calm. And ask yourself the right question: not «how much have I lost?», but **«if I didn't own it, would I buy it today at this price?»**.
steps.key: Losing hurts more than twice as much as winning feels good: that's why we cling on to losers.
steps.tip: The market doesn't care what you paid. Decide based on what you know today.

steps.title: What it is
steps.body:
The tendency to **sell winners too early** and **hold on to losers too long**.

Shefrin and Statman named it in 1985. Odean (1998) measured it across thousands of accounts: investors sold their winning shares much sooner than their losing ones.

steps.title: The worst part
steps.body:
The winners they sold went on to perform **better**, on average, than the losers they kept.

It's the exact opposite of the classic advice: **«cut your losses and let your profits run»**. In R terms: taking profits at +0.5R and letting losses run to −2R wrecks the expectancy of any system.

steps.title: How to protect yourself
steps.body: Stop and exit plan **before** you get in. If the trade goes your way, the plan decides the exit (for example, half at 2R and the rest with a trailing stop), not the fear of giving back what you've made.
steps.key: We sell winners for a quick buzz and hold losers so we don't have to admit a mistake.
steps.tip: Cut your losses and let your profits run. Your brain will ask you to do the opposite.

steps.title: The fear of missing out
steps.body:
**FOMO** kicks in when something shoots up and everyone seems to be making money. It's the engine of bubbles: dotcoms in 1999, crypto in 2017 and 2021, *meme stocks* in 2021.

**Herd behaviour** is following the crowd. But once **everyone** has already bought, there's nobody left to keep pushing the price up.

steps.title: Warning signs
steps.body:
• You hear about it from friends or social media accounts that had never invested before.
• The reason is «**it's going up a lot**», not what the asset actually does.
• You feel **urgency**: «if I don't buy today, I'll miss it».
• People say «**this time it's different**».

steps.title: How to protect yourself
steps.body:
• **The 48-hour rule:** any purchase outside your plan waits two days.
• A **speculation limit** written into your plan.
• Ask yourself: **«Would I buy it if nobody were talking about it?»**
steps.key: When everyone's talking about something that «only goes up», the risk is usually at its highest.
steps.tip: If your hairdresser recommends a cryptocurrency, it might already be too late.

steps.title: We think we know more than we do
steps.body:
• Barber and Odean (2000): the 20 % of households that traded most earned **11.4 %** a year versus **17.9 %** for the market.
• In another study (2001), men traded **45 % more** than women and cut their net returns by more.

The main cause: overconfidence.

steps.title: Luck or skill
steps.body:
A few winning trades early on are the most dangerous thing that can happen to a beginner: they **mistake luck for skill**, raise their risk and break their own rules.

Calling 4 out of 4 coin tosses happens 6.25 % of the time: among lots of people, there will always be some «geniuses».

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Now you're going to try to guess four real charts. Whatever your score, remember: with so few attempts, the result says almost nothing about your skill.
steps.key: Getting it right two or three times doesn't make you an expert: with few trades, luck is in charge.
steps.tip: Track your results in your journal and compare them with an index. Your memory always says you were right.

steps.title: Anchoring
steps.body:
Fixating on an irrelevant reference number: «It was at €100 and now it's at €60: it's cheap».

The past price says nothing about today's value. And a close relative: the **sunk cost**: «I've already lost €3,000, I can't sell now». What's lost won't come back: decide from today.

steps.title: Confirmation bias
steps.body:
Once you buy, you only read the good news, follow people who agree with you and dismiss the criticism. When the warning signs arrive, you don't see them.

Antidotes: write down **three reasons you could be wrong** and deliberately look for the **opposite view**.

steps.title: Your takeaway
steps.body: Value things with today's data (earnings, debt, business), not with the price you paid or the price it used to be.
steps.key: Falling a lot doesn't make something cheap. People agreeing with you doesn't make you right.
steps.tip: If you only read people who agree with you, you're not analysing: you're cheering yourself on.

steps.title: Recency
steps.body:
Giving too much weight to whatever happened last. After two years of rises, believing the market «always goes up»; after a fall, that it «will always go down».

Antidote: look at **decades of data**, not months. Japan's Nikkei took 34 years to get back to its 1989 peak; the S&P 500 recovered within months after covid.

steps.title: Survivorship bias
steps.body:
Only seeing the ones that survived. Funds that close vanish from the statistics; traders who lose everything don't post videos.

Bessembinder: since 1926, just **4 %** of US shares accounted for the market's entire net gain, and **more than half** returned less than Treasury bills.

steps.title: Your takeaway
steps.body: The success stories you see are a rigged sample: you don't see the thousands who did the same thing and failed.
steps.key: What's recent and what's visible aren't the whole story.
steps.tip: Before copying a winner, ask how many people did the same thing and lost.

u27l1-1.prompt: According to Morningstar, how much less a year did the average investor earn than their own funds over the 10 years to 2025?
u27l1-1.explanation: 9.9 % for the funds versus 8.7 % for their investors, from buying and selling at the wrong time.

u27l1-2.prompt: Which system is making the decision?
options: Working out your system's expectancy from your journal
Buying because everyone's talking about it
Selling everything after reading an alarming headline
Dodging an e-scooter coming straight at you
u27l1-2.explanation: System 1 is useful for survival; for investing, it pays to force yourself to use system 2.

u27l1-3.prompt: Kahneman's system 1 is slow and analytical.
u27l1-3.explanation: It's the fast, intuitive and emotional one. The slow, analytical one is system 2.

u27l1-4.prompt: Picture €10,000 over 10 years at 9.9 % a year (the fund) or at 8.7 % (its investors). How big is the difference at the end? (round to the nearest euro)
u27l1-4.explanation: 10,000 × 1.099¹⁰ ≈ €25,703 versus 10,000 × 1.087¹⁰ ≈ €23,030: about €2,673 lost purely to behaviour.

u27l1-5.prompt: One Monday you read: «Stock markets plunge 4 %». You have an index fund for 20 years from now and your heart is racing. What do you do?
options: Buy loads more with my whole emergency fund
Sell now, before it falls further
Take a breath, reread my plan and touch nothing today
u27l1-5.explanation: Big decisions should never be made with your heart racing.
feedback: Reacting with your emergency fund is also deciding in the heat of the moment.
That's system 1 in charge. This is how the investor gap is made: selling after the fall.
Good: you're giving system 2 time. One bad day doesn't change a 20-year plan.

u27l1-6.prompt: In spot bitcoin ETFs, what did investors get compared with the ETF itself?
options: Quite a bit more than the ETF
u27l1-6.explanation: They bought at the peaks and sold in the dips.

u27l1-7.prompt: Quick: where was the investor gap biggest?
options: It was the same across all of them
u27l1-7.explanation: −2.1 points in the most volatile versus −0.4 in the calm ones: more scares, more mistakes.

u27l1-8.prompt: What tends to put system 1 in charge? Select all that apply.
u27l1-8.explanation: A written checklist forces you to think slowly: it's a system 2 tool.

u27l1-9.prompt: The problem behind the gap isn't the product, it's the investor's ____.
u27l1-9.explanation: The same fund gives different results depending on how you get in and out.

u27l1-10.prompt: What do you explain to Lumi?
options: You probably got in and out at the wrong time: that's the investor gap
Funds always lie in their figures
u27l1-10.explanation: Your return depends on the fund and on when you get in and out.
feedback: Oops… I bought when it was at its highs and sold in the March scare. Touché.
Maybe not: if you got in after the rises and out in the falls, the difference is down to you.
The fund's performance figures are real; what changes is when you were invested.
lines: My fund has made 10 % a year… but I've made way less! 🤨

u27l2-1.prompt: According to prospect theory, a loss of €100 hurts roughly…
options: As much as winning €100 feels good
Twice as much as winning €100 feels good

u27l2-2.prompt: You're offered a coin toss: heads you win €150, tails you lose €100. What's the expected gain per toss?

u27l2-3.prompt: With that same coin (heads +€150, tails −€100), most people say no. Why?
options: Because the bet loses money on average
Because losing €100 hurts more than winning €150 feels good
u27l2-3.explanation: Loss aversion makes us turn down decisions with a positive expected value.
feedback: It's a fair coin: the explanation is in our heads.
On average it wins €25 per toss: the maths isn't the problem.
Exactly: loss aversion outweighs the positive expected value.

u27l2-4.prompt: If a loss hurts twice as much as a gain of the same size, how much would you need to win to emotionally make up for a loss of €100?
u27l2-4.explanation: €100 × 2 = €200: that's why many people only accept bets where the gain is double.

u27l2-5.prompt: Loss aversion makes us more reckless when we're losing.
u27l2-5.explanation: It's the «double up to win it back» move: we take on more risk to avoid locking in the loss.

u27l2-6.prompt: Marta has a share that's down 30 %. The company has cut its forecasts and lost its biggest customer. She says: «I'm not selling until I'm back to even». What question should she ask herself?
options: What are they saying on the forum?
If I didn't own it, would I buy it today at this price, knowing what I know?
How much have I lost already?
u27l2-6.explanation: The right decision looks at the business's future, not at your purchase price.
feedback: Looking for encouragement doesn't change the company's business.
Good: that way she decides with today's information, not her purchase price.
Focusing on what's been lost only feeds loss aversion.

u27l2-7.prompt: Quick: which habit makes myopic loss aversion worse?
options: Checking your long-term portfolio several times a day
u27l2-7.explanation: The more often you look, the more often you see red and the more you want to tinker with it.

u27l2-8.prompt: The key question: «If I didn't own it, would I ____ it today at this price?».
u27l2-8.explanation: It separates the decision from your purchase price.

options: I'm out because the stop I set earlier was hit
I turn down a bet with positive expected value because I'm scared of losing
I double my position to win it back sooner
I won't sell until I get back what I paid
I sell because the business has got worse
u27l2-9.explanation: Sound decisions look at the plan and the business; the others look at the pain of losing.

u27l2-10.prompt: What do you reply to Lumi?
options: Being wrong is normal; what matters is deciding with what you know today
Buy more to bring your average price down
Well done, hold on until it comes back
u27l2-10.explanation: Accepting a small loss in time is part of the game, not a failure.
feedback: You're right: the market doesn't know what I paid. I'll review the business, not my pride.
Averaging down without reviewing the business is putting more money into the same mistake.
Sometimes it doesn't come back. And while you wait, that money could be somewhere better.
lines: I'm not selling that share at a loss 😤
Selling would mean admitting I got it wrong.

options: Spreading your money across lots of assets
Selling winners too early and holding losers too long
Always buying whatever is rising most
u27l3-1.explanation: Odean measured it in 1998 across thousands of accounts.

u27l3-2.prompt: You buy at the last price with a €10,000 account and a maximum risk of 1 %. Set your stop now, calmly, before the price moves.
u27l3-2.explanation: Setting the stop before you get in stops loss aversion from convincing you to hold on «until it comes back» if the price falls.

u27l3-3.prompt: Another purchase with €10,000 and 1 % risk. Choose your stop and amount, and think: if it goes your way, would you exit out of fear or according to your plan?
u27l3-3.explanation: If the trade goes your way, the plan decides the exit, not the urge to lock in a small gain.

u27l3-4.prompt: Laura needs €2,000. She has share A up +20 % and share B down −20 % (company B has just reported poor results). What do most people do, and what would make sense?
options: Sell A because it's in profit
Decide based on each business's future, not on whether it's green or red
u27l3-4.explanation: What matters is what you expect from each asset, not your purchase price.
feedback: That's what almost everyone does: the disposition effect. She keeps the one that's getting worse.
Good: if B has got worse and A hasn't, the logical move may be the exact opposite of what your gut says.
Running away from everything doesn't fix the bias: it just swaps it for another one.

u27l3-5.prompt: According to Odean, the winning shares investors sold went on to do worse than the losing ones they kept.
u27l3-5.explanation: It was the other way round: the winners they sold kept performing better on average.

u27l3-6.prompt: A system is right 60 % of the time, but out of fear you close winners at +0.5R and let losers run to −2R. What's your expectancy?
u27l3-6.explanation: 0.6 × 0.5 − 0.4 × 2 = 0.3 − 0.8 = −0.5R. The disposition effect turns a good hit rate into losses.

u27l3-7.prompt: Disposition effect or following the plan?
options: Removing the stop because «it's nearly there»
Selling half at 2R, as the plan says
Exiting because the stop set before entry was hit
Selling at +5 % for fear of losing it
Holding a share at −40 % «until it comes back»
u27l3-7.explanation: The difference is who's deciding: the plan written calmly or the emotion of the moment.

u27l3-8.prompt: The classic advice: cut your losses and let your ____ run.
u27l3-8.explanation: The disposition effect does the exact opposite.

u27l3-9.prompt: Always selling what's in the green and holding what's in the red is a good way to manage a portfolio.
u27l3-9.explanation: That's the disposition effect: you cut what's working and feed what isn't.

options: Yes, lock it in, you never know
What did your exit plan say before you got in?
Buy more with everything you've got
u27l3-10.explanation: The exit is decided before you get in, not when you see the first bit of green.
feedback: It might work out today, but if you always do it, you cut short your best trades.
Hmm… It said half at 2R and the rest with a trailing stop. OK, I'll stick to the plan.
Swinging from fear to euphoria in a minute isn't a plan either.
lines: I'll sell it now, before it drops.

u27l4-1.prompt: Select the messages trying to trigger your FOMO to sell you something or trick you.
options: Reminder: your regular €100 contribution will go through on the 5th.
Everyone's making money on this share. Put your savings in, don't overthink it.
Only 3 places left in my signals group. This time it's different, don't miss out.
Check whether a firm is authorised before investing with it.
🚀 This crypto is up 300 % in a month. Tomorrow will be too late. Get in NOW!
u27l4-1.explanation: Urgency, «this time it's different» and «everyone's winning» are the classic signs of FOMO.

u27l4-2.prompt: November 2021: bitcoin is at record highs, it's on every news bulletin and your friends who had never invested are buying. What did it do next?
u27l4-2.explanation: Bitcoin fell by around 75 % over the following year. The moment of peak euphoria is usually the moment of peak risk. Remember: with crypto you can lose everything you put in.

u27l4-3.prompt: This asset has risen sharply and everyone on social media is talking about it. Does it go up or down over the following sessions?
u27l4-3.explanation: Neither the hype on social media nor the earlier rises tell you what's coming. That's why the 48-hour rule exists.

u27l4-4.prompt: A friend messages you: «This share is up 200 % in two weeks. Everyone in the group is in. Get in today!». It's not in your plan. What do you do?
options: Take out a loan to go in big
Buy now, before it rises further
Apply the 48-hour rule and ask myself whether I'd buy it if nobody were talking about it
u27l4-4.explanation: Urgency is FOMO's fuel: taking the time pressure off the decision is the antidote.
feedback: Debt + FOMO is the classic recipe for the worst losses.
You're buying out of FOMO: without knowing what the company does and after a huge rise.
Good: if it still makes sense in two days and fits within your speculation limit, you decide calmly.

options: Double your position if it keeps rising
Buy straight away so you don't miss the rise
Wait 48 hours on any purchase that isn't in your plan
u27l4-5.explanation: Two days is enough for the urgency to pass.

u27l4-6.prompt: Which are warning signs of a bubble? Select all that apply.
options: The only reason is that it's going up a lot
u27l4-6.explanation: Steady earnings aren't a sign of a bubble: euphoria and a lack of reasons are.

u27l4-7.prompt: Once everyone has already bought something, it usually has plenty of room left to rise.
u27l4-7.explanation: If everyone has already bought, there's nobody left to keep pushing the price up.

u27l4-8.prompt: Quick: which question protects you from herd behaviour?
options: How much has it gone up this week?
Would I buy it if nobody were talking about it?
What are they saying on the forum?
u27l4-8.explanation: It separates value from what the crowd is doing.

u27l4-9.prompt: Match each bubble with its era.
u27l4-9.explanation: The assets change; FOMO is always the same.

options: Wait 48 hours and think about whether you'd buy it if nobody were talking about it
u27l4-10.explanation: The rush is the signal: when you feel urgency, stop.
feedback: That's the one thing you never touch. And with crypto you can lose everything you put in.
OK… If it still makes sense in two days, I'll put it within my speculation limit. If not, nothing.
If I get in out of fear of missing out, I'll most likely buy near the top.
lines: Everyone on TikTok is making money on a new coin 🐶
If I don't get in today, I'll miss out.

u27l5-1.prompt: Round 1 of 4. Real chart, no name or date. Does it go up or down over the following sessions?
u27l5-1.explanation: One right or wrong answer on its own means nothing. Note it down and carry on: at the end you'll see what your score means.

u27l5-2.explanation: Two rounds is still a tiny sample, however you're doing.

u27l5-3.explanation: If you've got three right, careful not to feel like a genius; if you've got three wrong, you're not a disaster either. It's noise.

u27l5-4.explanation: With four attempts, getting them all right by chance happens more than once in twenty. To know whether you have an edge, you need lots of recorded trades.

u27l5-5.prompt: If you guess at random (50 %), what's the probability of getting 4 out of 4 right?
u27l5-5.explanation: 0.5⁴ = 0.0625 → 6.25 %. If 1,000 people try, about 62 will get them all right without knowing anything.

u27l5-6.prompt: According to Barber and Odean (2000), how much a year did the 20 % of households that traded most earn compared with the market?
u27l5-6.explanation: Trading more, out of overconfidence, cost them over 6 points a year.

u27l5-7.prompt: Quick: according to Barber and Odean (2001), how much more did men trade than women?
u27l5-7.explanation: And their net returns fell by more than women's.

u27l5-8.prompt: Winning your first trades proves you have skill.
u27l5-8.explanation: With only a few trades, luck counts for a huge amount. It's exactly when the danger of raising your risk is greatest.

u27l5-9.prompt: Bruno has got 3 trades in a row right in the simulator. He wants to triple his size «because he's got the hang of it now». What's going on?
options: Overconfidence: he should keep the same risk and keep recording
Nothing, three in a row prove he knows what he's doing
u27l5-9.explanation: After several wins, the rule stays the same: the risk per trade doesn't change.
feedback: Good: your risk per trade doesn't change because you're on a winning run.
Winning streaks don't remove the risk; they only hide it.
Three in a row by chance happens one time in eight. It proves nothing.

u27l5-10.prompt: What protects you from overconfidence? Select all that apply.
options: Writing down three reasons you could be wrong
Raising your risk after every win
Comparing yourself with an index over several years
Tracking your results in a journal
u27l5-10.explanation: Raising your risk after a win is exactly what overconfidence does.

u27l6-1.prompt: Match each bias with the phrase that gives it away.
u27l6-1.explanation: Each phrase sounds reasonable… until you spot the bias behind it.
right: «I only follow people who think like me»
«It's fallen seven days in a row, it's bound to go up tomorrow»
«I've already lost so much, I can't sell now»
«It was at €120, at €70 it's a steal»

u27l6-2.prompt: Match each bias with its antidote.
u27l6-2.explanation: Every mental shortcut has a question that takes it apart.
right: Decide from today, ignoring what's been lost
Remember that each day is almost independent

u27l6-3.prompt: «The share was at €120 and now it's at €70: it's going for a song». Which bias is this?
u27l6-3.explanation: The €120 is an anchor: it says nothing about the company's current value.

u27l6-4.prompt: Pablo bought at €40. Now it's worth €25 after poor results and a forecast cut. He says: «I'm not selling until it's back at €40». What's going on?
options: He's anchored to the €40 (with a side of sunk cost and loss aversion)
He should buy more to bring his average price down
He's right: the price will come back
u27l6-4.explanation: The price you paid isn't information about the future.
feedback: Exactly. He should ask himself: if I had €25 in cash today, would I buy this share knowing what I know?
Averaging down because of an anchor is putting in more money without reviewing the business.
It might come back or it might not; the €40 only matters to him, not to the market.

u27l6-5.prompt: Ana has bought a share. Since then she only reads bullish forums and mutes anyone who criticises the company. What habit would you recommend?
options: Write down three reasons she could be wrong and read opposing views
Carry on like this, it's good vibes
u27l6-5.explanation: You fight confirmation bias by deliberately looking for what contradicts you.
feedback: Good: if her reasons stand up to the criticism, great. If not, better to know now.
She doesn't need to sell: she needs to look at the other side.
Good vibes and bad decisions: she won't see the warning signs.

u27l6-6.prompt: The price you paid for a share affects what the market will do.
u27l6-6.explanation: The market doesn't care what you paid: it only matters to you.

u27l6-7.prompt: Quick: «I've already put €3,000 into this, I can't quit now». Which bias is this?
u27l6-7.explanation: What you've invested won't come back by carrying on: decide from today.

u27l6-8.prompt: Before buying, write down three reasons you could be ____.
u27l6-8.explanation: It's the simplest antidote to confirmation bias.

u27l6-9.prompt: A share falls from €100 to €60. If you anchor on the €100 and wait for it to come back, how much does it need to rise? (round to one decimal place)

u27l6-10.prompt: What do you reply to Lumi?
options: Cheap or expensive depends on what the business is worth, not on where the price used to be
Yes, half price is always a bargain
Wait for it to drop another 50 % and it'll be even cheaper
u27l6-10.explanation: Stock market sales aren't like supermarket sales: the product may have changed too.
feedback: True. First I'll look at earnings, debt and why it fell. The old price isn't a price tag.
Not in the stock market: it may have fallen because the business is worth half… or less.
That's still only looking at the price, not the value.
lines: It's half price, like in the sales!

u27l7-1.prompt: Look at just these two months of a real chart. What trend do you see? (Microsoft · closes every 3 sessions · June–August 2026)
u27l7-1.explanation: It's clearly rising. Recency makes us believe it will always carry on like this; a two-month stretch says nothing about the coming years.

u27l7-2.prompt: This is how Japan's Nikkei was doing up to November 1989. Tap the highest point. (Nikkei 225 · monthly closes · up to 30/11/1989)
u27l7-2.explanation: After years of rises, everyone thought it would carry on. The late-1989 peak took 34 years to get back to.

u27l7-3.prompt: September 1929: the US stock market has been rising for years and «everyone» is buying, many with borrowed money. What did the S&P 500 do next?
u27l7-3.explanation: The fall reached over 80 %. What had happened in the previous years didn't predict what was coming.

u27l7-4.prompt: After two years of strong rises, Laura believes the market «always goes up» and puts all her savings in. Which bias is she mainly showing?
u27l7-4.explanation: She's giving too much weight to what has just happened (and there's probably some overconfidence too).

u27l7-5.prompt: According to Bessembinder, most US shares since 1926 returned more than Treasury bills.
u27l7-5.explanation: More than half returned less. Just 4 % accounted for the market's entire net gain.

u27l7-6.prompt: You see ten people on social media who got rich from a small cryptocurrency. Which conclusion is correct?
options: Buying small cryptos is a safe way to get rich
It's survivorship bias: I don't see the people who did the same and lost everything
If ten of them managed it, so can I
u27l7-6.explanation: Success stories are a biased sample: the graveyard of those who didn't make it is missing.
feedback: You only see the ones who won. The thousands who lost don't post about it.
Good: visible winners say nothing about your odds. And with crypto you can lose everything.
Ten winners among hundreds of thousands isn't a high probability.
